hints: Look closely at what you can actually see in A compared to B - does one show only the outside surface while the other lets you see inside the cell?
walkthrough:
Picture What Each Microscope Does**
Think of SEM as taking a photograph of the outside of an object. Electrons bounce off the surface, so you get a sharp 3-D looking image with lots of depth, but you cannot see inside. TEM is like slicing very thin and shining light through - electrons pass through the section, so you get a flat 2-D image of the inside.

Match To Fig. 1.1**
In A the microvilli look like fingers sticking up with shadows and depth and you see only their outer surface, with no organelles visible below. In B you see a flat slice right through the top of the cell, so you can see inside the cytoplasm with mitochondria and other structures below the microvilli. That contrast tells you A is SEM and B is TEM.

Final answer: Fig. 1.1A is a scanning electron micrograph showing a 3-D surface / outer view of microvilli, while Fig. 1.1B is a transmission electron micrograph showing a 2-D thin section through the cell showing internal structures.

hints: Start from the rule $magnification = image size / actual size$ - what two values do you need in the same units to use it here?
Think about how to get a reliable image size for tiny microvilli and how to handle mm on your ruler versus $\mu m$ for the real length.
walkthrough:
Get a Fair Image Size**
Use a ruler to measure the length of a microvillus from base to tip on the printed Fig. 1.1. Because they vary a little, measure several microvilli and calculate a mean to be more reliable. Do this separately for A and for B because magnifications differ.

Use $M = I / A$ With Matching Units**
The formula is $magnification = \frac{image\ length}{actual\ length}$. Your ruler gives mm but actual length is $1 \mu m$. Convert so both are in the same units, for example convert mm to $\mu m$ by multiplying by 1000. Then divide the mean image length by $1 \mu m$ to get magnification, which has no units.

Final answer: Measure the length of a microvillus on the image in mm, measure several and calculate a mean. Convert to same units as actual size ($1 \mu m$). Magnification = image length / actual length.

hints: Apart from using ATP, what is unusual about the direction active transport can move a substance compared to diffusion?
Think about the protein itself - how does it pick out only Na+ or K+ and what must happen to its shape to push them through?
walkthrough:
Direction That Needs Energy**
Diffusion and facilitated diffusion can only go down a gradient from high to low. Active transport is special because with energy from ATP it can pump a water-soluble ion uphill from low to high concentration, which is exactly what the Na+/K+ pump does to keep Na+ low inside.

How The Carrier Does It**
The carrier protein has specific binding sites that are complementary in shape to the ion, so only that ion fits. When the ion and phosphate from ATP bind, the protein changes shape - a conformational change - which carries the ion across and releases it on the other side.
Final answer: Movement against a concentration gradient / from low to high concentration; via specific complementary binding sites with conformational / shape change of carrier protein.

hints: Compare glucose inside the cell to glucose in the gut lumen after the pump has worked - which way would glucose want to move on its own?
Look at what Na+ is doing at the same protein - which way is Na+ moving and how could that downhill flow help drag glucose uphill?
walkthrough:
The Problem For Glucose**
The Na+/K+ pump keeps pumping Na+ out, so Na+ is high in the gut lumen and low in the cell. Glucose builds up inside the cell, so glucose needs to move from the lumen where it becomes low into the cell where it is higher - that is uphill against its gradient and needs an energy source.

Using The Sodium Gradient As Power**
Na+ wants to rush back in down its steep gradient from lumen to cell by facilitated diffusion through the cotransporter. The cotransporter couples the two movements together, so the downhill inward flow of Na+ powers the uphill inward flow of glucose. This is indirect active transport - ATP is used at the pump, not at the cotransporter itself.

Final answer: Glucose is moving into the cell against its concentration gradient so cannot enter by diffusion alone; entry is coupled to Na+ moving down its concentration gradient into the cell by facilitated diffusion, providing energy for cotransport.

hints: Think about folding a flat membrane into hundreds of tiny fingers - what does that do to the total area facing the gut lumen?
Link that extra membrane area to the proteins shown in Fig. 1.2 - what more can fit in if there is more membrane?
walkthrough:
More Membrane In The Same Space**
Each microvillus is a tiny finger-like fold of cell surface membrane. Hundreds of them hugely increase the total surface area exposed to the gut lumen without taking up much more space.

More Doors For Glucose**
Glucose and Na+ can only enter through cotransporter proteins in the membrane. A larger membrane can hold many more of these transport proteins, so more glucose can be cotransported per unit time, increasing the rate of uptake.
Final answer: Microvilli greatly increase surface area of the cell surface membrane, so more cotransport / carrier proteins for Na+ and glucose can be located in the membrane for faster uptake.

hints: Think about life in the gut - with acid, enzymes and friction from food, what happens to the epithelial cells lining it?
Recall what mitosis always produces - what is the genetic relationship between parent and daughters and why does that matter for function?
Stem cells have two jobs when they divide - making specialised cells and looking after themselves - what must happen for both?
Put it together into a chain: damage leads to need for new cells, new cells need to work properly, and the supply must continue.
walkthrough:
Constant Wear Needs Replacement**
The small intestine is a harsh place with mechanical abrasion, acid and enzymes. Epithelial cells are easily damaged and short-lived, so continuous mitosis replaces old, dead or damaged cells to repair and maintain the lining.

Making Identical, Specialisable Cells**
Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells with the same DNA, so they can function normally and safely differentiate into specialised intestinal cells such as absorptive cells with microvilli. Some daughters remain as stem cells, replenishing the stem cell pool so division can continue.

Growth As Well As Maintenance**
In a growing person extra cells are also needed to increase the size of the intestine. Together, replacement, production of identical cells able to specialise, and renewal of stem cells explain why continuous mitosis is vital.

Final answer: To replace old / dead / damaged cells to repair tissue; to produce cells that can differentiate into specialised intestinal epithelial cells; daughter cells are genetically identical to parent for normal function; for growth and to replenish / maintain stem cell numbers.
